name: Mixing ratio
seoTitle: Mixing ratio Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: Mixing ratio: work out substance 12 from the substance 1 and the substance 2. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Mixing ratio calculator the substance 1, the substance 2, the substance 3 and the substance 4 and it returns substance 12. Think of it as a shortcut for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Mixing ratio calculator work?
sections.html:
The Mixing ratio calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports substance 12 in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the substance 1, the substance 2, the substance 3 and the substance 4.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Mixing ratio calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Substance 12=-substance 1 − substance 10 − substance 11 − substance 13 − substance 14 − substance 15 − A16 − substance 2 − substance 3 − substance 4 − substance 5 − substance 6 − substance 7 − substance 8 − substance 9 + suma

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Mixing ratio calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the substance 1, the substance 2 and the substance 3 — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Mixing ratio calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — substance 1 for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Re-enter the same figure and confirm the result is stable; a number that moves when you press Calculate again is a sign that a field is still empty.

faq.q: What does the Mixing ratio calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns substance 12, derived from the substance 1, the substance 2 and the substance 3. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Mixing ratio calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the substance 1, the substance 2, the substance 3 and the substance 4, which is 18 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Suma = 0. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Mixing ratio calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
